newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela assuages U.S. fears over Kinshasa democracy.
newsitem.headline: Mandela assuages U.S. fears over Kinshasa democracy.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela told visiting U.S. congressmen on Wednesday they need not fear a dictatorship in the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire.

"I just want to assure you that we understand and appreciate the concern about democracy in that country," he said. "Because of my association with President (Laurent) Kabila, I have no such fear at all because of the steps that he has taken already."
Mandela's government was among the first to recognise Kabila after he declared himself president following the capture of Kinshasa 11 days ago by his rebel forces.
The South African leader has taken pains in recent days to play down Western concerns about Kabila's democratic credentials and his refusal to schedule elections immediately in the country.

Speaking in Cape Town, Mandela told the bi-partisan U.S. delegation led by Congressman Ed Royce of California, that Kabila had asked the people of Kisangani in eastern Zaire to elect local representatives a few days after his forces captured the third-largest town on March 15.
Also in the delegation were Congressmen Robert Menendez of New Jersey, Alcee Hastings of Florida, Bobby Rush of Illinois and Congresswomen Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas and Maxine Waters of California.

Mandela also pointed out that after the capture of Kinshasa on May 19, Kabila's victorious alliance said it would convene a constituent assembly in 60 days to draft a constitution for the interim period until elections were held -- probably within two years.
In addition, Mandela said, Kabila had called on his people not to exact revenge against members of ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko's governing clique.
Opposition supporters and Western diplomats this week condemned Kabila's ban on demonstrations and political activity, accusing him of being no better than Mobutu.
